Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Titre d'origine : Unlocking supervisory effectiveness in credit risk: insights from the ECB’s supervisory findings and measures

ARTICLE :
Working Paper Series 
Unlocking supervisory effectiveness in 
credit risk: insights from the ECB’s 
supervisory findings and measures 
Alessandra Agati, Adele Fontana, 
João Matos Leite, Claudia Schwarz 
Disclaimer: This paper should not be reported as representing the views of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. 
No 3308 / November 2026 
 
 
Abstract 
This paper provides an assessment of supervisory effectiveness in credit risk using confidential 
data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis covers 8,106 supervisory measures issued 
and closed between 2016 and 2025. A central contribution is the constr uction of a measure-
level indicator of supervisory effectiveness based on large language model (LLM) analysis of 
supervisory narratives and closure justifications. The indicator captures whether supervisory 
measures resulted in full remediation of the underlying deficiencies. Using logistic and duration 
models, we examine the characteristics of findings, measures, and banks associated with 
remediation outcomes and remediation speed. The results show that multi-faceted findings are 
a key driver of supervisory outcomes. Measures related to data, reporting, and IT deficiencies 
are less likely to achieve full remediation and require longer remediation periods. Measures 
originating from on -site inspections are associated with higher remediation rates and faster 
closure. Stronger governance is also associated with more successful remediation outcomes. 
 
 
Keywords: supervisory effectiveness, credit risk, large language models, banking 
supervision 
JEL classifications: G21, E51, H81, G28 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
1
Non-technical summary 
Effective banking supervision requires more than identifying weaknesses in banks. It also 
requires ensuring that banks address those weaknesses in a timely and comprehensive 
manner. Yet assessing whether supervisory actions actually lead to remediation rem ains 
challenging. Supervisory performance is often measured through completed processes and 
activities, while evidence on whether supervisory interventions resolve the underlying 
deficiencies is much more limited. 
This paper provides new evidence on supervisory effectiveness in the area of credit risk using 
confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision. The analysis is based on more than 8,100 
supervisory measures issued and closed between 2016 and 2025 and recorded in the ECB's 
Findings and Measures database. The paper focuses on whether supervisory measures 
achieved their intended objective, namely the remediation of the deficiencies identified by 
supervisors. 
A key challenge is that remediation outcomes are not directly recorded in structured 
supervisory data. Although a measure may be formally closed, closure does not necessarily 
imply that the underlying issue has been fully resolved. To address this challeng e, the paper 
applies large language models (LLMs) to supervisory narratives and closure justifications to 
classify measures according to whether they resulted in full, partial, or no remediation. This 
creates a novel outcome -based indicator of supervisory effectiveness that can be analysed 
systematically across a large number of supervisory cases. 
Using this indicator, the paper examines which characteristics of supervisory measures, 
findings, and banks are associated with successful remediation and the time required to 
achieve it. 
The results show that supervisory effectiveness differs substantially across both measure 
types and institutions. 
First, the complexity of the underlying finding is an important determinant of outcomes. 
Measures addressing multiple issues are less likely to achieve full remediation and take longer 
to close. Similarly, deficiencies related to data, reporting and IT systems are among the most 
difficult to remediate, both in terms of success rates and remediation time. This reflects the 
substantial organisational, technological, and operational changes often required to address 
such weaknesses. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
2
 
 
Second, measures originating from on -site inspections are associated with more successful 
and faster remediation than measures resulting from broader supervisory processes such as 
the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) or ongoing supervisory monitoring. 
This finding suggests that highly targeted and in-depth supervisory assessments can facilitate 
corrective action and highlights the importance of using different supervisory tools in a 
complementary manner. 
Third, more severe supervisory measures are less likely to achieve full remediation and 
generally remain open for longer periods. This likely reflects the fact that more severe findings 
are often associated with deeper -rooted weaknesses and require more ex tensive corrective 
action. 
Fourth, bank characteristics matter, although their influence is generally weaker than that of 
finding and measure characteristics. Banks with stronger governance frameworks and those 
with higher profitability tend to achieve higher remediation rates . However, some of these 
relationships become less pronounced once differences across supervisory teams and 
institutions are taken into account, suggesting that remediation outcomes are influenced by a 
combination of bank-specific and supervisory factors. 
The results have several implications for supervisory authorities. They highlight the importance 
of designing supervisory measures that are sufficiently focused, clearly communicated, and 
tailored to the nature of the underlying deficiency. They also point to the particular challenges 
posed by complex, cross-cutting issues, especially those involving data and IT infrastructures, 
where remediation may require longer time horizons and sustained supervisory follow -up. 
More generally, the results can support supervisors in allocating resources and calibrating 
supervisory intensity more effectively. 
Beyond the substantive findings, the paper demonstrates how artificial intelligence can support 
supervisory effectiveness assessments. By transforming large volumes of unstructured 
supervisory information into structured data, LLMs make it possible to eval uate supervisory 
outcomes at a level of granularity that would otherwise be difficult to achieve. While the results 
should be interpreted as evidence of associations rather than causal effects, they provide a 
new and practical framework for monitoring and analysing supervisory effectiveness in banking 
supervision. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
3
 
 
1. Introduction 
The Global Financial Crisis and subsequent episodes of banking stress highlighted the 
importance of effective banking supervision and triggered far -reaching reforms of regulatory 
and supervisory frameworks. These reforms included revisions to the Capital Requi rements 
Directive and Capital Requirements Regulation, as well as the establishment of the Single 
Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in 2014 under the auspices of the European Central Bank 
(ECB). More recently, the banking turmoil of March 2023 renewed attention on the role of 
supervision in identifying vulnerabilities and ensuring that banks address them in a timely 
manner. 
But what defines effective supervision, and how can it be assessed? The Basel Committee on 
Banking Supervision (BCBS, 2025) defines supervisory effectiveness as: “Effective 
supervision promotes the safety and soundness of banks and the banking system by promptly 
assessing prudential risks, identifying material shortcomings within banks, and using the 
supervisory toolkit and powers appropriately to ensure that banks remediate shortcomings in 
a timely manner.” Effectiveness extends beyond compliance, focusing on timely intervention, 
corrective action, and institutional resilience. The BCBS identifies two key purposes for 
assessing supervision: public accountability and optimi sing supervisory strategy, such as 
determining which tools to use for different banks and how to allocate resources. Crucially, 
effectiveness should be measured by outcomes, not just outputs, as what matters is whether 
a bank’s remedial actions resolve identified shortcomings. 
Importantly, supervisory effectiveness should not be equated with changes in observed risk 
metrics. Supervisory measures rarely seek to reduce a specific level of credit risk directly. 
Instead, they typically aim to address weaknesses in governance arrange ments, risk -
management processes, internal controls, methodologies, data quality, reporting frameworks, 
or other prudential deficiencies. Consequently, a supervisory measure should be considered 
effective when the bank successfully implements the required corrective actions and 
remediates the identified shortcoming. In fact, effective supervision may sometimes lead to a 
temporary increase in measured risk if improved methodologies, controls, or reporting 
practices result in more accurate risk identification. For this reason, the focus of this paper is 
on remediation outcomes rather than subsequent changes in credit risk indicators or prudential 
metrics. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
4
 
 
Despite a growing literature on supervisory effectiveness, evidence on supervisory outcomes 
remains limited. Existing studies typically evaluate supervisory tools by examining their impact 
on bank behaviour, lending activity, risk-taking, or market outcomes. While these approaches 
provide valuable insights, they do not address a more granular question: whether individual 
supervisory measures achieve the remediation of the specific deficiencies they were intended 
to correct. Answering this question has prove d difficult because the relevant information is 
rarely available in structured datasets and often remains embedded in confidential supervisory 
documentation. 
This paper addresses that gap using confidential data from ECB Banking Supervision's 
Findings and Measures (F&M) database. The database contains detailed information on 
supervisory findings and measures generated through on-site inspections, horizontal reviews, 
ongoing supervisory activities, and the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP). 
Although the database contains more than 75,000 observations since the establishment of the 
SSM, much of the relevant information is stored in unstructured narr ative fields, making 
systematic analysis challenging. 
To overcome this challenge, we apply large language models (LLMs) to transform supervisory 
narratives into structured analytical variables. We first classify supervisory findings and 
measures into thematic categories using a dedicated taxonomy framework. We then construct 
a novel measure-level indicator of supervisory effectiveness by analysing supervisory closure 
narratives and classifying measures according to whether they resulted in full, partial, or no 
remediation of the underlying deficiency. This approach allows us to move beyond traditional 
process-based measures of supervision and towards an outcome -oriented assessment of 
supervisory effectiveness. 
Our analysis focuses on 8,1 06 credit-risk-related supervisory measures issued and closed 
between 2016 and 2025. Using the LLM -based effectiveness indicator, we examine which 
characteristics of supervisory measures, findings, and supervised institutions are associated 
with successful remediation in a logistic regression framework. We then analyse the duration 
of fully effective measures to identify the factors associated with faster or slower remediation 
using Cox proportional hazards model. 
Three main findings emerge. First, finding complexity is an important determinant of 
supervisory outcomes. Measures addressing multiple issues are less likely to achieve full 
remediation and remain open for longer periods. Data, reporting, and IT -related deficiencies

5
 
 
also prove particularly difficult to remediate. Second, supervisory measures arising from on -
site inspections exhibit higher remediation rates and shorter remediation periods than 
measures originating from broader supervisory processes such as the SREP or ongoing 
supervisory monitoring. Third, bank characteristics matter, albeit to a lesser extent than finding 
and measure characteristics. Stronger governance and greater profitability are associated with 
better remediation outcomes, although these relationsh ips weaken once supervisory -team 
heterogeneity is considered. 
This paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it provides one of the first large -
scale empirical assessments of supervisory effectiveness at the level of individual supervisory 
measures rather than supervisory frameworks or instruments. Se cond, it introduces a novel 
outcome-based measure of supervisory effectiveness grounded in the remediation of identified 
deficiencies. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence can be used to extract policy -
relevant information from large volumes of confidential supervisory text, thereby expanding the 
scope for empirical research and policy evaluation in banking supervision. 
The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on 
supervisory effectiveness and textual analysis. Section 3 describes the methodology and the 
construction of the LLM-based effectiveness indicator. Section 4 presents the data. Section 5 
discusses the empirical results. Section 6 concludes. 
2. Literature review 
This study draws on two strands of research. The first is the empirical literature on the 
effectiveness of banking supervision, reviewed in Section 2.1. The second is the literature on 
textual data and artificial intelligence in economics and finance, reviewed in Section 2.2. This 
paper is at the intersection of the two : a granular, measure -level assessment of supervisory 
effectiveness, made possible by applying large language models to a large body of 
unstructured supervisory text. 
2.1 Evaluating supervisory effectiveness 
The most comprehensive recent survey of this field is the Basel Committee's literature review 
on supervisory effectiveness (BCBS, 2025). It organises the evidence around a 'house of 
effectiveness': a set of enablers and impediments at the base, three pilla rs: risk identification 
and assessment, remediation and enforcement, and collaboration and transparency and 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
6
 
 
supervisory culture as the roof. This section follows that structure, after first setting out what 
effectiveness means and why it is hard to measure. 
2.1.1 Risk identification and assessment 
The first pillar concerns the tools through which supervisors identify and assess risk: on -site 
inspections, supervisory stress tests, horizontal reviews and benchmarking, and early-warning 
models (BCBS, 2025). On -site inspections have received the most em pirical attention, 
because they are intrusive and may involve a detailed review of the loan book. The Basel 
Committee's review reports that inspections promote more conservative risk management, 
with more prudent provisioning afterwards, and that the supervisory ratings derived from them 
have predictive power for financial stress (BCBS, 2025). Consistent with this, Passalacqua et 
al. (2021) use the quasi-random selection of Italian banks for inspection and find that inspected 
banks are more likely to reclassify loans as non-performing, cut credit to unproductive 'zombie' 
firms, and reallocate lending towards more productive borrowers, with positive spillovers for 
the wider economy; they trace these effects to improvements in bank governance. Bonfim et 
al. (2023) report comparable results for inspections of the largest Portuguese banks, although 
in that case the effect was confined to the inspected portfolios. Importantly, supervisory 
activities often extend beyond risk identification and contribute directly to remediation. The 
distinction between assessing weaknesses and ensuring their correction is therefore not 
always clear-cut. 
2.1.2 Remediation and enforcement 
The second pillar concerns the tools through which supervisors ensure that banks correct 
identified weaknesses and comply with prudential requirements. These include capital 
constraints under Pillar 2, enforcement and sanction actions, early -intervention regimes, and 
individual accountability regimes (BCBS, 2025). For a study focused on credit risk, the 
evidence on sanctions is particularly relevant. The Basel Committee's working paper finds that 
enforcement actions promote a more truthful classification of credit quality, reduce bank risk 
and lending, and generate deterrent effects on non -sanctioned banks, with effectiveness 
increasing in severity and depending critically on timing (BCBS, 2025). 
Prior studies find that supervisory sanctions and capital -related supervisory measures can 
reduce risk-taking and strengthen resilience, although their effectiveness depends on timing, 
severity and institutional context (Delis et al., 2016; Caiazza et al., 2018; Berger et al., 2022; 
BCBS, 2025). This literature is the closest precedent for the present study, yet a gap remains. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
7
 
 
Each of these studies measures the response of the bank, or of credit supply, to an 
enforcement tool. None measures whether a specific supervisory measure was implemented, 
and the underlying shortcoming rectified. Whether a measure achieves its purpose is unlikely 
to be uniform: a narrowly targeted measure may be more readily remedied than a broad one, 
and a bank with stronger governance, may comply more readily than a weaker peer. 
These remain conjectures because the evidence does not reach the level of the individual 
measure. As a result, little is known about which categories of findings are remediated, which 
are not, and which characteristics of banks and supervisory measures dis tinguish the two 
outcomes. 
Other dimensions of supervisory effectiveness, including coordination, transparency, 
consistency and supervisory culture, have also received attention in the literature. For 
example, Agarwal et al. (2014) show that differences in supervisory practices acro ss 
authorities can lead to inconsistent regulatory outcomes, while the BCBS (2025) highlights the 
roles of supervisory cooperation, transparency and organisational culture in supporting 
effective oversight. These dimensions are important determinants of supervisory outcomes but 
are less directly related to the measure-level focus of this paper. 
Taken together, the literature shows that the effectiveness of supervision depends on the tools 
used, on the bank, and on the institutional setting. What it does not provide is evidence at the 
level of the individual measure and its remediation . The binding constraint is not a lack of 
observations, but their form and confidentiality: the relevant information is recorded as free text 
rather than structured data and is typically not publicly accessible. This limitation is therefore 
less about data availability than about the ability to analyse them systematically. Turning 
unstructured supervisory text into analysable variables, and so into outcome-level evidence, is 
the methodological problem addressed in the next section. 
2.2 Textual analysis and artificial intelligence 
A key reason why effectiveness remains difficult to assess is that some of the richest 
supervisory records are stored as free text, inspection reports, findings, and the narratives that 
justify supervisory decisions , which conventional statistical methods cannot readily exploit. 
Advances in textual analysis, particularly through artificial intelligence, make it possible to 
convert this information into structured data, thereby enabling large-scale empirical analysis of 
supervisory outcomes that would otherwise be prohibitively time -consuming. Text-as-data 
approaches have become increasingly common in economics and finance, enabling 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
8
 
 
researchers to extract information from large collections of documents that would otherwise be 
difficult to analyse systematically (Gentzkow et al., 2019). 
Early applications relied primarily on dictionary -based approaches, which classify text using 
predefined word lists. While useful, these methods often struggle to capture context -specific 
meanings in financial and supervisory language (Loughran and McDonal d, 2011). More 
recently, machine learning techniques and large language models (LLMs) have substantially 
expanded the scope of textual analysis by allowing information to be interpreted in context and 
classified with greater flexibility (Huang et al., 2023; BIS, 2024; Korinek, 2023). 
These methods are increasingly being applied to central banking and financial stability 
analysis. Studies have shown that textual information contained in central bank publications 
can provide useful signals regarding perceptions of risk and future financi al vulnerabilities 
(Correa et al., 2021). Recent work at the ECB further demonstrates the potential of LLMs to 
identify and quantify risk assessments in financial stability communication and related policy 
documents (Fell et al., 2026). Applications to supervisory records remain comparatively limited, 
largely because such information is confidential. One notable exception is Goldsmith-Pinkham, 
Hirtle and Lucca (2016), who analyse the content of US supervisory examination reports and 
show that supervisory narratives contain information beyond formal supervisory ratings. 
However, existing studies have generally focused on characterising supervisory 
communication rather than assessing the outcomes of supervisory actions. 
2.3 Research gap and contribution 
The two strands reviewed above leave a specific gap. While the supervisory effectiveness 
literature provides evidence on the impact of broad supervisory tools, it rarely assesses 
whether individual measures lead to the remediation of underlying deficiencies . This reflects 
the distinction between supervisory outputs, i.e. completed supervisory actions, and 
supervisory outcomes, i.e. effective remediation. At the same time, textual -analysis methods 
have rarely been applied to the outcomes of confidential supervisory actions. 
Using confidential supervisory data from ECB Banking Supervision, we apply large language 
models to identify whether individual measures resulted in full, partial or no remediation. This 
allows an outcome-oriented assessment of supervisory effectiveness at the measure level and 
provides evidence on the characteristics of supervisory measures and banks associated with 
more effective remediation outcomes. 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
9
 
 
3. Methodology 
This section describes the methodology used to extract supervisory information from textual 
records through large language models and to quantify supervisory effectiveness at the 
measure level. 
3.1 Constructing the Effectiveness Variable Using Large Language 
Models 
A key empirical challenge is that supervisory effectiveness, i.e. whether a measure achieves 
its intended objective, is not directly observable in structured supervisory data. While the F&M 
database records supervisory actions and their administrative status, the closure of a measure 
does not necessarily imply that the underlying deficiency has been fully remediated. Measures 
may be closed despite only partial remediation, because they are superseded by new 
measures, or for other supervisory reasons. Consequently, a measure's closure status cannot 
be interpreted as a direct indicator of supervisory effectiveness. 
The information required to assess remediation is instead contained in qualitative supervisory 
narratives, particularly in the descriptions of identified shortcomings and in the justifica

Time Trends: Finally, the year of measure creation is significantly associated with remediation 
outcomes. Relative to measures created in 2016, measures initiated in most subsequent years 
exhibit a higher probability of full remediation, with particularly pronounced ef fects for 
measures opened in 2019 and during 2023 -2024. This pattern may reflect changes in 
supervisory practices, remediation processes, and follow -up intensity over time. It is also 
consistent with a stronger supervisory focus on the timely remediation of findings in the post-
pandemic period. Since 2022, ECB Banking Supervision has strengthened its approach to 
findings and measures through the introduction of escalation frameworks, additional guidance 
for Joint Supervisory Teams (JSTs), and enhanced suppo rt for the management of complex 
remediation cases. In parallel, JSTs were encouraged to place greater emphasis on the follow-
up of supervisory findings within their supervisory priorities and planning processes. However, 
these results should be interpreted with caution, as the sample includes only closed measures. 
More recent years may therefore be disproportionately represented by measures that were 
less complex and could be remediated within a shorter period. 
Robustness analyses: Several robustness checks were conducted to assess the stability of 
the baseline results. First, the model was re-estimated alternatively including JST and country 
fixed effects. Second, an alternative binary logit model excluding ineffective outcomes was 
estimated. Third, a multinomial logit specification was estimated to distinguish explicitly 
between full remediation, partial remediation, and ineffective outcomes . Across all 
specifications, the results remain qualitatively unchanged and continue to provide strong 
support for the main findings regarding finding complexity, topic area, measure severity, and 
process originator. Detailed results are reported in Annex 2.

5.2 Drivers of measure duration 
Table 2 reports the results of a Cox proportional hazards model explaining the time required 
to close fully effectively remediated supervisory measures i.e. a subset of all closed measures. 
Finding characteristics: The number of topics addressed within a measure is negatively 
associated with the speed of closure. Measures covering multiple topics require significantly 
longer remediation periods, suggesting that more complex findings are inherently more difficult 
to r esolve. This result is consistent with the notion that addressing several interconnected 
deficiencies often requires broader organisational changes, greater coordination across 
business areas, and more extensive supervisory follow-up. 
The nature of the underlying deficiency also plays an important role. Measures related to Data, 
Reporting & IT exhibit the longest remediation periods, while all other finding categories are 
associated with significantly faster closure. In particular, Gove rnance & Controls, NPE & 
Collateral Management, and Credit Lifecycle Management findings tend to be resolved more 
quickly. Remediation actions involving data infrastructures, reporting frameworks, and IT 
systems frequently require substantial investments, system development, and implementation 
efforts across multiple functions. By contrast, corrective actions targeting governance 
arrangements, credit processes, provisioning practices, or collateral management can often 
be implemented within shorter timeframes, resulting in faster remediation. 
The results indicate that the originator of the supervisory process is an important determinant 
of remediation speed. Relative to measures stemming from on -site inspections (OSI), 
measures originating from the SREP, Horizontal analyses, and JST activities exhibit 
significantly lower closure hazards, implying longer remediation periods. One possible 
explanation is that findings arising from broader supervisory assessments often relate to more 
structural or cross-cutting deficiencies, which may require more extensive remediation efforts 
before closure can be granted. 
Measure characteristics: 
Measure severity is also strongly associated with remediation duration. Compared with 
moderately severe measures (M2), low-severity measures (M1) are remediated more quickly, 
while high-severity (M3) and very high -severity (M4) measures remain open for lon ger. This 
pattern is consistent with the view that more severe findings typically reflect more significant 
ECB Working Paper Series No 3308
22
 
 
underlying weaknesses and therefore require more complex corrective actions and 
supervisory verification. 
By contrast, legal enforceability does not appear to affect remediation timelines. 
Recommendations do not differ significantly from legally binding obligations in terms of closure 
speed, suggesting that, conditional on other measure characteristics, the fo rmal legal status 
of a measure is not a key determinant of how quickly remediation is achieved. 
Bank characteristics: Among bank-level factors, higher credit risk materiality and greater 
profitability are associated with faster remediation. This may indicate that institutions for which 
credit risk is a more central area of activity, and those with stronger financial performance, are 
better positioned to allocate resources to the implementation of corrective actions. However, 
these relationships weaken substantially once country and JST fixed effects are introduced, 
suggesting that part of the observed association reflects persistent differences across 
supervised institutions or supervisory teams rather than independent effects of these bank 
characteristics. 
By contrast, weaker governance, as measured by a higher SREP Governance score, is 
associated with faster closure among fully effective measures. This result should be interpreted 
cautiously. As shown in Section 5.1, weaker -governance banks are less likely to achieve full 
remediation in the first place. Since the duration analysis is conditional on successful 
remediation, the result may partly reflect selection effects, whereby only a subset of measures 
with a relatively high likelihood of remediation reache s closure in weaker -governance 
institutions. It may also reflect supervisory prioritisation, with both banks and supervisors 
focusing remediation efforts on a smaller number of measures where successful completion is 
considered most achievable.

Robustness analyses: One potential concern is that the estimated relationships may be 
influenced by unobserved differences across supervised institutions, supervisory teams or 
national supervisory environments. To address this, the Cox model was re-estimated 
including alternatively country and JST fixed effects. In particular, the estimated effects of 
finding complexity, finding type, process originator and measure severity remain stable 
across specifications. By contrast, the estimated effects of credit risk materiality, profitability 
and governance weaken substantially once JST fixed effects are included. This suggests that 
part of the variation attributed to bank characteristics in the baseline specification reflects 
persistent differences across supervised institutions or supervisory teams. 
In addition, the proportional hazards diagnostics reported in Annex 3 indicate violations of the 
proportional hazards assumption for several covariates and for the model globally. Hence, as 
an additional robustness check, Annex 4 reports estimates from a Weibull Accelerated Failure 
Time (AFT) model, which does not rely on this assumption. 
The AFT specification confirms the main findings of the Cox model. Measures associated with 
a larger number of findings exhibit significantly longer remediation durations, while findings 
related to Governance & Controls, Classification & Staging, Provisioning & Model Risk, NPE 
& Collateral Management, and Credit Lifecycle Management are closed more rapidly than 
findings in the reference category. SREP -originated measures are estimated to remain open 
approximately 4% longer than otherwise comparable measures, whereas measures 
originating from Horizontal functions and JSTs a lso exhibit modestly longer remediation 
durations. Weaker governance scores and higher credit risk materiality are asso ciated with 
significantly shorter closure times, while legal enforceability continues to have no statistically 
significant effect. Although some individual coefficients differ in magnitude from those obtained 
in the Cox model, the overall pattern of results remains unchanged.

Taken together, the consistency of the results across alternative specifications, including the 
AFT model and the additional bank -level controls, provides further evidence that the main 
conclusions are robust. 
6. Conclusion 
This paper provides a granular, outcome-oriented assessment of supervisory effectiveness by 
focusing on the remediation of supervisory measures in credit risk. Using a novel application 
of LLM to confidential supervisory data, it constructs a measure-level indicator of effectiveness. 
Further, using the subset of fully effectively closed measures, a duration analysis is conducted. 
Both analyses assess drivers using measure characteristics and bank -specific factors 
providing a comprehensive narrative about their influence on remediation outcomes. 
Finding issue : The results show that finding complexity is an important determinant of 
supervisory outcomes. Measures addressing a larger number of topics are less likely to 
achieve full remediation and take substantially longer to close. In addition, Data, Reporting & 
IT findings emerge as particularly challenging to remediate. Relative to other finding types, 
such measures display both lower remediation rates and longer remediation horizons, 
highlighting the implementation challenges associated with data quality, reporting frameworks 
and IT infrastructures. Findings originating from on -site inspections outperform those 
stemming from broader supervisory activities, such as the SREP and ongoing JST 
assessments, both in terms of remediation rates and closure times. 
Measure Characteristics: Supervisory measure characteristics are strongly associated with 
both effectiveness and remediation speed. More severe measures are less likely to achieve 
full remediation and require longer implementation periods. Recommendations are associated 
with a hig her likelihood of full remediation, although legal enforceability does not appear to 
influence remediation speed. Taken together, these findings suggest that the nature of the 
underlying deficiency, the supervisory tool employed, and the complexity of impl ementation 
are important correlates of supervisory outcomes. 
Bank characteristics : Bank characteristics play a more nuanced role. More profitable 
institutions and banks with greater credit -risk materiality display stronger remediation 
outcomes in the baseline specifications, although these relationships weaken once JST -
specific heterogen eity is considered. By contrast, weaker governance is consistently 
associated with a lower likelihood of full remediation. At the same time, among measures that 
are fully remediated, weaker-governance institutions tend to achieve closure more quickly, a

result that may reflect selection effects or supervisory prioritisation rather than a direct 
governance effect on remediation speed. 
Time and Temporal Trends: The results indicate that measures initiated in most years after 
2016 are more likely to achieve full remediation, with particularly strong improvements 
observed in recent years. This pattern is consistent with an increased supervisory focus on 
remediation and follow-up, including the introduction of dedicated escalation frameworks and 
supervisory guidance supporting the closure of findings. 
Policy Implications : The findings offer several actionable insights for supervisors and 
policymakers: 
Simplifying Complex Measures : The greater effectiveness of recommendations and on -site 
measures may suggest that simplifying the implementation of measures could improve 
compliance. Supervisors should focus on feasibility, particularly for less well -resourced or 
poorly governed institutions. 
Tailoring Supervisory Strategies: Supervisors should account for bank-specific characteristics, 
such as governance, when designing and enforcing measures. The findings suggest that 
remediation strategies may need to be tailored to the characteristics and implementation 
capacity of supervised institutions. 
More broadly, the paper demonstrates how artificial intelligence can support the systematic 
evaluation of supervisory outcomes by transforming large volumes of unstructured supervisory 
information into empirically usable data. While the analysis identifies associations rather than 
causal effects and relies on documented remediation captured in supervisory narratives, it 
provides a practical framework for monitoring supervisory effectiveness at scale and 
contributes new evidence to the growing policy discussion on how supervisory success should 
be measured.
